short_definition: Delayed gratification is the ability to resist a smaller, immediate reward in order to receive a larger or more lasting reward later, a skill central to saving, investing and long-term goals.
explanation: Delayed gratification is best known from the 'marshmallow' studies led by psychologist Walter Mischel at Stanford starting in the 1960s. In those studies, children could eat one treat right away or wait to get two. Later research suggested that the link between waiting as a child and outcomes later in life is weaker than first reported once family background is taken into account. It is better understood as a skill shaped by environment and strategy than as a fixed trait.

Delayed gratification matters because most money and self-development goals pay off later, whether that is saving money, studying for a qualification or building a business. The costs come now and the benefits come later, so anything that makes waiting easier improves your odds of following through.

Delaying everything isn't wise either. Spending on health, relationships and experiences now has real value, and an overly strict plan is often hard to stick with and can lead to spending binges. Practical strategies include automating savings, removing temptations (such as card details saved in shopping apps), waiting 24 or 48 hours before non-essential purchases, and budgeting some guilt-free spending money.
example: Illustrative example: you are tempted by a $1,200 phone upgrade. Instead, you keep your current phone for another year and set up an automatic $100 monthly transfer to savings. After 12 months you have $1,200 plus any interest. You can then buy the phone outright, or put the money toward a bigger goal, without taking on debt.
common_mistake: Relying on willpower alone. People who are good at delaying gratification usually change their environment, through automation, hiding temptations and waiting periods, instead of fighting the same temptation over and over.
title: Delayed Gratification
